name: Behavioral Science
description: An interdisciplinary exploration of the biological, psychological, and social forces that shape human and animal behavior, with applications to health, economics, and society.

modules.title: Introduction to Behavioral Science
modules.objectives: Define behavioral science as an interdisciplinary field, identify its major subfields, and distinguish it from pure psychology or biology.
modules.readingNote: NIH Office of Behavioral and Social Sciences Research — definition and multilevel scope of behavioral and social science.

modules.assignment: Use the NIH OBSSR definition to analyze a fictional school problem: lunch participation fell after the cafeteria schedule, menu, and peer-group seating changed. Create a systems map with biological/individual, psychological/behavioral, social, environmental, and policy factors; propose two measurable research questions and identify one discipline that would inform each. Submit: systems map plus 250–350 words. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: interdisciplinary accuracy, causal caution, measurable questions, and evidence that does not reduce behavior to one level.

modules.title: Evolutionary Psychology
modules.objectives: Apply natural selection principles to explain evolved psychological mechanisms, evaluate the evolutionary basis of altruism, mate selection, and aggression.
modules.readingNote: GIIS module lesson — evolutionary hypotheses, evidence, limitations, and avoidance of adaptation-only explanations.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.

modules.assignment: Choose one behavior from this set—fear learning, cooperation, food preference, or jealousy—and write a 350–450 word evolutionary hypothesis. State the proposed ancestral problem, predicted mechanism, two testable predictions, one plausible non-evolutionary explanation, and one modern mismatch or limitation. Submit: hypothesis table plus analysis. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: testability, distinction between explanation and justification, consideration of alternatives, and avoidance of claims that a trait is universal or optimal merely because it may be adaptive.

modules.title: Behavioral Genetics
modules.objectives: Explain heritability, distinguish between twin and adoption study methods, and evaluate the nature-nurture interaction in traits like intelligence and personality.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §3.1 — genes, environment, heritability, twin/adoption logic, and gene–environment interplay.

modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional study: identical twins raised apart correlate .65 on a trait, fraternal twins raised together correlate .30, and the sample comes from one country and age group. Explain what the pattern can and cannot show about genetic influence. Submit: a 350–450 word methods memo defining heritability, describing twin/adoption logic, identifying shared/nonshared environment and at least three limitations, and proposing one follow-up design. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: population-level interpretation, no genetic determinism, correct comparison logic, and justified limitations.

quizQuestions.question: Behavioral science is best described as:
options: A subfield of medicine focused on drug therapy
An interdisciplinary field studying behavior through biology, psychology, and social science
The study of animal behavior only
quizQuestions.answer: An interdisciplinary field studying behavior through biology, psychology, and social science
quizQuestions.explanation: Behavioral science integrates biology, psychology, sociology, and other fields to understand human and animal behavior.

quizQuestions.question: Which discipline is NOT typically considered part of behavioral science?
quizQuestions.answer: Astronomy
quizQuestions.explanation: Astronomy studies celestial objects and has no direct connection to behavioral science.

quizQuestions.question: Which research question is most clearly multilevel behavioral science?
options: How does sleep duration alone predict attendance when the school setting is held constant?
How do sleep, beliefs, peer norms, and school schedules jointly affect attendance?
What percentage of students attend on each weekday?
Does changing the menu alter reported food preference?
quizQuestions.answer: How do sleep, beliefs, peer norms, and school schedules jointly affect attendance?
quizQuestions.explanation: Behavioral science integrates processes within individuals with social and environmental influences on observable behavior or health-relevant outcomes.

quizQuestions.question: Evolutionary psychology proposes that psychological mechanisms evolved because they:
options: Increased reproductive success in ancestral environments
quizQuestions.answer: Increased reproductive success in ancestral environments
quizQuestions.explanation: Evolutionary psychology applies natural selection: psychological traits persisted because they improved survival and reproduction.

quizQuestions.question: The concept of inclusive fitness explains why organisms may sacrifice themselves for:
quizQuestions.answer: Genetically related relatives
quizQuestions.explanation: Hamilton's inclusive fitness theory explains altruism toward kin as benefiting shared genes.

quizQuestions.question: Sexual selection theory predicts that females will be more selective in mate choice because:
options: Their parental investment is typically greater
quizQuestions.answer: Their parental investment is typically greater
quizQuestions.explanation: Parental investment theory (Trivers) holds that the sex with greater investment (females in most species) is more selective in choosing mates.

quizQuestions.question: What would make an evolutionary explanation scientifically stronger?
options: Assuming every common behavior is adaptive
Stating testable predictions and comparing them with plausible alternatives
Treating current usefulness as proof of ancestral selection
quizQuestions.answer: Stating testable predictions and comparing them with plausible alternatives
quizQuestions.explanation: Evolutionary hypotheses need evidence, falsifiable predictions, and comparison with learning, cultural, developmental, or by-product explanations.

quizQuestions.question: Heritability refers to the proportion of variance in a trait attributable to:
options: Genetic differences among individuals in a population
The total genetic makeup of an individual
quizQuestions.answer: Genetic differences among individuals in a population
quizQuestions.explanation: Heritability is a population-level statistic indicating how much of the variability in a trait is due to genetic differences.

quizQuestions.question: Monozygotic twins share approximately what percentage of their DNA?
quizQuestions.explanation: Monozygotic (identical) twins develop from one fertilized egg and share virtually 100% of their DNA.

quizQuestions.question: Adoption studies test genetic influences on behavior by:
options: Comparing adopted children to their biological vs. adoptive parents
quizQuestions.answer: Comparing adopted children to their biological vs. adoptive parents
quizQuestions.explanation: If adoptees resemble biological parents more than adoptive parents, it suggests genetic influence on that trait.

quizQuestions.question: Before any conditioning, food powder naturally causes a dog to salivate. In this pre-training phase, the salivation is the:
quizQuestions.answer: Unconditioned response
quizQuestions.explanation: Before learning, food is the unconditioned stimulus and the reflexive salivation it elicits is the unconditioned response.

quizQuestions.question: Stimulus generalization in classical conditioning occurs when:
options: The original CS no longer produces a CR
Similar stimuli to the CS also elicit the CR
The organism distinguishes between two similar stimuli
The response increases with repeated pairings
quizQuestions.answer: Similar stimuli to the CS also elicit the CR
quizQuestions.explanation: Generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli similar to the original CS with the same CR.

quizQuestions.question: Taste aversion is a special case of classical conditioning because it:
options: Can be acquired in a single trial with a long delay between CS and UCS
quizQuestions.answer: Can be acquired in a single trial with a long delay between CS and UCS
quizQuestions.explanation: Taste aversions violate typical conditioning rules by forming in a single trial even with hours between CS (food) and UCS (illness).

quizQuestions.question: Counterconditioning, used to treat phobias, involves:
options: Flooding the person with feared stimuli
Pairing the feared stimulus with a positive response to replace the fear
quizQuestions.answer: Pairing the feared stimulus with a positive response to replace the fear
quizQuestions.explanation: Counterconditioning (as in systematic desensitization) replaces a conditioned fear response by associating the CS with relaxation.

quizQuestions.question: Positive punishment involves:
options: Adding a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior
Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase behavior
Adding an unpleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
Removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
quizQuestions.answer: Adding an unpleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
quizQuestions.explanation: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus following a behavior, decreasing the likelihood of its recurrence.

quizQuestions.question: In Operant Conditioning, Shaping uses:
options: Successive approximations to reinforce behaviors closer to the goal
quizQuestions.answer: Successive approximations to reinforce behaviors closer to the goal
quizQuestions.explanation: Shaping reinforces progressively closer approximations to the target behavior until the full behavior is acquired.

quizQuestions.question: Which example is negative reinforcement?
options: Removing an unpleasant alarm when a seat belt is fastened
Adding extra chores after rule breaking
Taking away game time after missed work
quizQuestions.answer: Removing an unpleasant alarm when a seat belt is fastened
quizQuestions.explanation: Negative reinforcement increases a behavior because that behavior removes or avoids an aversive stimulus; it is not punishment.

quizQuestions.question: Which schedule typically produces high, persistent responding because reinforcement follows an unpredictable number of responses?
quizQuestions.answer: Variable ratio
quizQuestions.explanation: A variable-ratio schedule reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses and often produces steady, extinction-resistant responding.

quizQuestions.question: Cognitive distortions, as identified in CBT, are:
options: Habitual irrational thought patterns that contribute to negative emotions
quizQuestions.answer: Habitual irrational thought patterns that contribute to negative emotions
quizQuestions.explanation: Cognitive distortions (e.g., catastrophizing, all-or-nothing thinking) are inaccurate thoughts that maintain psychological distress.

quizQuestions.question: In Ellis's ABC model, 'B' refers to:
options: Belief or self-talk about the event
quizQuestions.answer: Belief or self-talk about the event
quizQuestions.explanation: In REBT's ABC model: A = activating event, B = belief/interpretation, C = emotional and behavioral consequence.

quizQuestions.question: Cognitive restructuring in CBT involves:
options: Identifying and challenging maladaptive thought patterns
Exposure to feared stimuli without cognitive work
quizQuestions.answer: Identifying and challenging maladaptive thought patterns
quizQuestions.explanation: Cognitive restructuring teaches clients to identify cognitive distortions and replace them with more balanced, realistic thoughts.

quizQuestions.question: In Ellis's ABC model, what does C represent?
quizQuestions.answer: The emotional and behavioral consequences
quizQuestions.explanation: A is the activating event, B is the belief or interpretation, and C is the resulting emotional and behavioral consequence.

quizQuestions.question: Vicarious reinforcement occurs when:
options: A person is directly rewarded for a behavior
A person increases a behavior after observing someone else being rewarded for it
quizQuestions.answer: A person increases a behavior after observing someone else being rewarded for it
quizQuestions.explanation: Vicarious reinforcement — seeing a model rewarded — increases the observer's likelihood of performing the same behavior.

quizQuestions.question: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment demonstrated that children:
options: Will not imitate aggression they observe
Imitate aggressive behaviors they observe in adults
Only imitate behaviors that are directly reinforced
Become less aggressive after watching violent models
quizQuestions.answer: Imitate aggressive behaviors they observe in adults
quizQuestions.explanation: Bandura's study showed children who watched an adult hit a Bobo doll spontaneously imitated the aggressive behaviors.

quizQuestions.question: Which experience most directly builds self-efficacy?
options: Repeated mastery of progressively challenging tasks
Watching a model fail without explanation
quizQuestions.answer: Repeated mastery of progressively challenging tasks
quizQuestions.explanation: Successful mastery experiences are a particularly strong source of confidence that one can perform a behavior.

quizQuestions.question: A token economy is based on which principle of operant conditioning?
quizQuestions.answer: Generalized conditioned reinforcement
quizQuestions.explanation: Tokens are generalized conditioned reinforcers — neutral stimuli paired with many backup reinforcers — making them broadly motivating.

quizQuestions.question: A functional behavior assessment (FBA) is used to identify:
options: The intelligence level of a student
The function or purpose that a problem behavior serves for the individual
quizQuestions.answer: The function or purpose that a problem behavior serves for the individual
quizQuestions.explanation: FBA determines what environmental triggers and consequences maintain a behavior, informing individualized intervention.

quizQuestions.question: Differential reinforcement of alternative behavior (DRA) involves:
options: Punishing problem behavior and ignoring alternative behavior
Reinforcing an alternative appropriate behavior while withholding reinforcement for problem behavior
Using shaping to increase problem behavior frequency
quizQuestions.answer: Reinforcing an alternative appropriate behavior while withholding reinforcement for problem behavior
quizQuestions.explanation: DRA replaces problem behavior by reinforcing a more acceptable behavior that serves the same function.

quizQuestions.question: In an ABC observation, the consequence is:
options: The event immediately before the behavior
What happens immediately after the behavior
A permanent diagnosis of why it occurred
quizQuestions.answer: What happens immediately after the behavior
quizQuestions.explanation: ABC recording describes antecedent, behavior, and consequence. Repeated patterns can support a functional hypothesis but do not prove function from one observation.

questions.question: Which field is considered the foundation of modern behavioral science?
questions.answer: Psychology
questions.explanation: Psychology is the primary disciplinary foundation of behavioral science, providing methods, theories, and empirical findings.

questions.question: Kin selection theory explains altruistic behavior toward relatives as driven by:
options: Shared genetic interest — helping relatives propagates shared genes
questions.answer: Shared genetic interest — helping relatives propagates shared genes
questions.explanation: Hamilton's rule: altruism toward kin is favored by natural selection because it increases inclusive fitness through shared genes.

questions.question: Twin studies showing identical twins raised apart are more similar than fraternal twins raised together provide evidence for:
options: The influence of shared family environment
Strong genetic contributions to trait variance
questions.answer: Strong genetic contributions to trait variance
questions.explanation: MZA twins sharing genetics but not environment being similar suggests genetic factors drive variance in those traits.

questions.question: After a conditioned response has been extinguished, it briefly returns when the conditioned stimulus is presented after a rest period. This is:
questions.answer: Spontaneous recovery
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response after time has passed, showing that extinction does not simply erase the original learning.

questions.question: Which research question most clearly integrates individual beliefs, interpersonal support, and environmental access in one multilevel behavioral-science study?
options: How does neural reward response predict exercise choice within one laboratory task?
How does peer support interact with beliefs and neighborhood access to affect exercise?
Does one reminder message increase step counts during a single week?
Which neighborhoods have the largest number of recreation facilities?
questions.answer: How does peer support interact with beliefs and neighborhood access to affect exercise?
questions.explanation: The selected question links an individual factor (beliefs), an interpersonal factor (peer support), and an environmental factor (neighborhood access) to the same behavior.

questions.question: An evolutionary hypothesis should be treated as scientific when it:
options: Generates testable predictions and survives comparison with alternatives
Assumes current behavior was directly selected
questions.answer: Generates testable predictions and survives comparison with alternatives
questions.explanation: Scientific evolutionary accounts require falsifiable predictions, relevant evidence, and evaluation against competing explanations.

questions.question: Why does a high heritability estimate not mean a trait is fixed?
options: Heritability applies only to one person
Heritability describes variation in a population under particular environments, and environments can still change outcomes
questions.answer: Heritability describes variation in a population under particular environments, and environments can still change outcomes
questions.explanation: Heritability is population- and context-specific; it does not measure immutability or the genetic percentage of an individual trait.

questions.question: Which comparison most directly supports a twin-study estimate of genetic influence?
options: Identical and fraternal twin similarity under carefully considered environmental assumptions
Two unrelated people from different countries
Parents and children who share both genes and home without controls
questions.answer: Identical and fraternal twin similarity under carefully considered environmental assumptions
questions.explanation: Comparing monozygotic and dizygotic twin similarity helps estimate genetic contribution, though equal-environment and sampling assumptions must be examined.

questions.question: After conditioning, a tone similar to the original conditioned stimulus also elicits fear. This is:
questions.answer: Stimulus generalization
questions.explanation: Generalization occurs when stimuli resembling the conditioned stimulus evoke a similar conditioned response.

questions.question: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when:
options: The conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus
A reward is removed after behavior
The conditioned stimulus is paired with a larger unconditioned stimulus
questions.answer: The conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented without the unconditioned stimulus
questions.explanation: Repeated CS presentations without the UCS weaken the conditioned response, although recovery can occur later.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly labels classical conditioning after learning?
questions.answer: CS → CR
questions.explanation: After acquisition, the previously neutral stimulus has become the conditioned stimulus (CS), and it now elicits the learned conditioned response (CR) without the unconditioned stimulus being presented.

questions.question: Stimulus discrimination is demonstrated when an organism:
options: Responds equally to every similar stimulus
Responds to the trained CS but not to a distinct safe cue
questions.answer: Responds to the trained CS but not to a distinct safe cue
questions.explanation: Discrimination is learning to distinguish the conditioned stimulus from other cues that do not predict the unconditioned stimulus.

questions.question: Which limitation should be considered when interpreting twin studies?
options: The equal-environments assumption may not fully hold
Heritability is identical in every population
questions.answer: The equal-environments assumption may not fully hold
questions.explanation: If identical twins experience more similar environments than fraternal twins, some similarity attributed to genes may reflect environment.

questions.question: Which statement avoids the naturalistic fallacy in evolutionary psychology?
options: If a behavior evolved, it is morally right
An evolved tendency can be studied without treating it as desirable or inevitable
Every cultural norm is genetically fixed
questions.answer: An evolved tendency can be studied without treating it as desirable or inevitable
questions.explanation: Explaining a possible origin does not justify a behavior morally or show that it is fixed or beneficial today.

questions.question: Heritability coefficients can only be interpreted in the context of:
options: A specific population in a specific environment
questions.answer: A specific population in a specific environment
questions.explanation: Heritability is a population statistic that varies depending on the genetic and environmental variability present in that sample.

questions.question: Which consequence is positive reinforcement?
options: Adding praise after a completed task and seeing task completion increase
Adding an unpleasant chore to reduce lateness
questions.answer: Adding praise after a completed task and seeing task completion increase
questions.explanation: Positive reinforcement adds a valued consequence after behavior and increases the future probability of that behavior.

questions.question: A behavior increases because it stops an unpleasant noise. This is:
questions.answer: Negative reinforcement
questions.explanation: The behavior is strengthened by removal of an aversive stimulus, which defines negative reinforcement.

questions.question: Shaping is most useful when:
options: The target behavior already occurs reliably
The target can be built by reinforcing successive approximations
No observable behavior can be defined
questions.answer: The target can be built by reinforcing successive approximations
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces steps that become progressively closer to a target behavior.

questions.question: Negative punishment (response cost) involves:
options: Adding an unpleasant event to decrease behavior
Removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase behavior
Adding a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior
questions.answer: Removing a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior
questions.explanation: Negative punishment removes something valued (privileges, tokens) contingent on the unwanted behavior, decreasing it.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Cognitive behavioral approaches differ from pure behaviorism by emphasizing:
options: The mediating role of thoughts and beliefs in behavior
questions.answer: The mediating role of thoughts and beliefs in behavior
questions.explanation: CBT includes learning principles but also examines how thoughts and beliefs shape emotion and behavior.

questions.question: Bandura's concept of self-regulation involves:
options: The capacity to set standards, monitor behavior, and adjust it toward goals
questions.answer: The capacity to set standards, monitor behavior, and adjust it toward goals
questions.explanation: Self-regulation is the internally driven process of goal setting, self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and self-reinforcement.

questions.question: Which is the best behavioral experiment for the belief “If I ask one question, everyone will think I am incompetent”?
options: Ask one prepared question, record actual responses, and compare them with the prediction
Repeat the belief until it feels true
Ask someone else to guarantee the outcome
questions.answer: Ask one prepared question, record actual responses, and compare them with the prediction
questions.explanation: A behavioral experiment states a prediction, tests it safely, and compares observable results with the original belief.

questions.question: Observational learning is most likely when the learner:
options: Attends, remembers, can reproduce the act, and has motivation
Receives punishment before seeing the model
questions.answer: Attends, remembers, can reproduce the act, and has motivation
questions.explanation: Bandura identified attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation as core processes in observational learning.

questions.question: Vicarious punishment occurs when:
options: A person’s own behavior is rewarded
Seeing a model punished makes the observer less likely to imitate the behavior
Tokens are exchanged for backup reinforcers
questions.answer: Seeing a model punished makes the observer less likely to imitate the behavior
questions.explanation: Observed consequences can change the observer’s future behavior even without direct reinforcement or punishment.

questions.question: Why should a functional behavior assessment use repeated data across contexts?
options: One observation always proves the function
Patterns across antecedents and consequences support a more defensible hypothesis
Behavior has the same function for everyone
questions.answer: Patterns across antecedents and consequences support a more defensible hypothesis
questions.explanation: Repeated observations help distinguish reliable contingencies from coincidence; the result remains a testable functional hypothesis.

questions.question: Differential reinforcement of alternative behavior works by:
options: Reinforcing an appropriate replacement while withholding the maintaining consequence for problem behavior when safe
questions.answer: Reinforcing an appropriate replacement while withholding the maintaining consequence for problem behavior when safe
questions.explanation: DRA teaches and reinforces a safer behavior that can meet the same function, while the plan addresses the prior contingency.

questions.question: Maintenance of behavior change in ABA requires strategies like:
options: Thinning reinforcement schedules and building natural community reinforcement
questions.answer: Thinning reinforcement schedules and building natural community reinforcement
questions.explanation: For maintenance, ABA practitioners thin reinforcement gradually and program behavior to contact naturally occurring reinforcers in the environment.

questions.question: Which answer best completes this statement? Reciprocal determinism (Bandura) differs from strict behaviorism by recognizing that:
options: Behavior, personal factors, and environment influence each other
Cognition has no role in behavior
questions.answer: Behavior, personal factors, and environment influence each other
questions.explanation: Bandura's reciprocal determinism describes ongoing interaction among behavior, cognition/personal factors, and environment.

questions.question: Which plan best supports generalization of a new behavior?
options: Teach it with one person in one room only
Practice with varied people, settings, and cues while reinforcing successful transfer
Change the target definition each day
questions.answer: Practice with varied people, settings, and cues while reinforcing successful transfer
questions.explanation: Generalization improves when the skill is practiced and reinforced across relevant contexts and natural cues.

questions.question: A behavior analyst conducting an FBA observes that a student's tantrums result in being sent to the hallway. This suggests the behavior is maintained by:
options: Escape or avoidance of task demands
questions.answer: Escape or avoidance of task demands
questions.explanation: If tantrums result in leaving the classroom, the behavior is negatively reinforced by escape from aversive academic demands.

questions.question: What is the purpose of fading in a behavior-change plan?
options: Gradually transfer control from prompts or dense rewards to natural cues and consequences
Remove all support before the skill is learned
questions.answer: Gradually transfer control from prompts or dense rewards to natural cues and consequences
questions.explanation: Fading reduces added prompts or reinforcement carefully so the behavior persists under natural conditions.

questions.question: A student begins using a study planner after seeing a respected peer praised for organized work. Which process best explains the change?
questions.answer: Vicarious reinforcement
questions.explanation: The observer is more likely to imitate the modeled behavior after seeing the model receive a valued consequence, which is vicarious reinforcement.

questions.question: Self-efficacy for a health behavior is most effectively increased by:
options: Watching others fail at the behavior
questions.answer: Mastery experiences (successfully performing the behavior)
questions.explanation: Bandura identified mastery experiences as the most powerful source of self-efficacy — nothing builds confidence like actual success.

questions.question: Sensory reinforcement in ABA refers to behavior maintained by:
options: Automatic sensory feedback produced by the behavior itself
questions.answer: Automatic sensory feedback produced by the behavior itself
questions.explanation: Automatically reinforced behaviors produce sensory consequences (e.g., rocking, hand-flapping) that are intrinsically reinforcing.

questions.question: When a behavior plan does not improve the target behavior, the best next step is to:
options: Check measurement and implementation fidelity, reassess the functional hypothesis, and revise the plan
questions.answer: Check measurement and implementation fidelity, reassess the functional hypothesis, and revise the plan
questions.explanation: Data-based practice checks whether the plan was implemented as designed and whether the functional hypothesis still fits before revising intervention.
